hook: You know the verse about being crucified with Christ. But did you know it comes right after Paul tells how he rebuked Peter to his face?
story:
Picture a table in Antioch. Jews and non-Jews who follow Jesus are eating together, and Peter is one of them. Then some people arrive from James, and Peter “drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.” The fear is named in the text. Others follow him, “so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy.”

Paul does not let it pass quietly. “I resisted him to his face,” he writes to the Galatians, and he spoke to Peter “before them all”. His question is about the table: “why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?” Then he goes on, and in the World English Bible the speech runs without a break through the words about being justified “by faith in Christ” and not by the law, and into this verse: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

To the people who first heard this letter, the word “crucified” was not a gentle picture. A Roman orator named Cicero, prosecuting a governor in a courtroom, spoke of a Roman citizen named Gavius who was beaten with rods and then crucified at Messana on a cross set where it looked toward the strait, so that he could see Italy and his home across the water. Cicero called it a deed so guilty that no name was bad enough for it. Paul chose that word for himself, and he later told the Galatians that Jesus Christ had been “openly portrayed among you as crucified”.

The people he wrote to, the Galatians, took their name from Gauls who had crossed into Asia Minor around 278 B.C. and been given land there. By Paul’s day Rome had made it a province.

moment:
Paul is writing a letter, and he writes plainly. A few teachers had persuaded the Galatians that they needed circumcision and the Law of Moses to be complete in Christ. The Galatians were puzzled, and had begun to keep Jewish festivals. Paul calls them “Foolish Galatians” and asks, “Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?”

To make his case he tells them his own story. He had once been “more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers” and had “persecuted the assembly of God and ravaged it”. He tells them about a meeting in Jerusalem where James, Cephas and John gave him and Barnabas “the right hand of fellowship”, and then about the day at Antioch when the right hand of fellowship was tested at a dinner table.

All of this stands behind “it is no longer I who live”. It is not a quiet line from a devotional book. It is Paul answering a question that was dividing a church: what must a person bring to belong to God?
around:
Just before the verse Paul says, “I through the law died to the law, that I might live to God.” Just after it he adds, “I don’t reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!”

The verse closes with something easy to skip: the life he now lives, he says, he lives “by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.” The sentence that begins with a death ends with love, and it is written in the first person.
after:
Acts never mentions the incident at Antioch. It does record a break between Paul and Barnabas: Paul and Barnabas disagreed over taking Mark, and “the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other.” Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus, and Paul chose Silas. The sources do not tie that break to the dinner table.

How the Galatians answered Paul’s letter, the Bible does not say. What the Bible does show is Peter speaking of Paul years later: a letter in Peter’s name calls him “our beloved brother Paul” and says that some things in his letters “are hard to understand”. Another letter in Peter’s name is sent through “Silvanus, our faithful brother” and sends greetings from “Mark, my son”, two names tied to Paul’s mission. A BYU essay reads such details as signs of the bond between the two.

Later church tradition says the two taught together in Rome. Tradition is all that can be said of it here.
readings:
Many readers hear the verse as a statement about union with Christ: the old self has come to an end and Christ now lives in the believer. Paul says something close to it elsewhere, that “our old man was crucified with him”.

Others hear it first as the heart of an argument about how a person is made right with God. In the verses before, Paul writes that “a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ”, and this verse describes what that looks like from the inside.

A third question is a quiet one about the text itself. The World English Bible puts everything from verse 14 to verse 21 inside one speech, as if Paul said it all to Peter at Antioch. A reader can fairly ask how much of it was said that day and how much Paul shaped for the Galatians as he wrote. The passage does not mark the point where the one gives way to the other.
argued:
The scene at Antioch has been argued over since the early church. Jerome thought the confrontation between Paul and Peter was staged, and Augustine rejected that reading. Acts, which tells of a council in Jerusalem, never mentions a clash between the two. And we have only Paul’s side: the New Testament does not give Peter’s account. In a courtroom, Cicero once described crucifixion of a citizen in words that show how the Roman world heard the word: [[cicero]]

How it ended is read in more than one way too. The Catholic Encyclopedia holds that Peter’s silence suggests he agreed with Paul. A BYU essay instead reads the clash as a sign that the question of table fellowship was still being worked out by the church, not yet settled.
point: The verse is often hung on a wall as a private promise. In its setting it grows out of an argument about a shared meal, and it ends on the one “who loved me and gave himself up for me.”
lesson:
You may have met this verse as a line about trying harder, or about disappearing. In its setting it says nearly the opposite. Paul is not asking the Galatians to earn a place. He is pointing them to the one who “loved me and gave himself up for me”.

That can be a relief if you are tired of proving yourself. It can also be a challenge: Peter, a leader of the church, let fear of other people pull him away from a table, and Paul said so to his face.

If you want to sit with this, read Galatians 2 slowly from the table at Antioch to the end of the chapter, and ask where you have been tempted to ask a person to bring more than the grace of God asks of them. And if you do not share this faith, the scene still shows something real: how much a community changes when belonging stops depending on a checklist.

echoes.note: Paul comes back to the same cross at the end of the letter: “the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” The boast is in what Christ did, not in what the Galatians could add.
In another letter Paul says “our old man was crucified with him”, and ties it to no longer being in bondage to sin. The thought is the same, joined to Christ’s death.
Paul says Christ “died for all” so that “those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him”. It is the same turn from living for yourself to living by Christ.
